title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about putting creative methods to work in your academic study. By the end you will be able to use visual and mapping methods to generate and organise ideas, generate several approaches to a task and adapt when one is not working, and bring imaginative thinking to how you analyse and interpret sources.

Creativity is not a decoration on academic work, nor a gift that some people have and others do not. It is a set of methods you can learn and use, and it is named among the attributes universities and employers value most. These lessons give you methods you can apply to real tasks straight away.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: use creative methods to generate and organise ideas for academic work
generate several approaches to a task and adapt your approach when one is not working
apply imaginative thinking to analyse and interpret academic material.

title: In real academic practice
body: Creative methods are not a side activity; they are how good academic work gets started and kept on track. Every assignment you plan, every problem you work through, every source you interpret draws on generating ideas, staying flexible and reading imaginatively. Build these methods now and they serve every project of your degree, and the creative problem-solving that professional work rewards.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, generating and organising ideas with visual methods such as mind mapping. Second, thinking flexibly: producing several approaches to a task and adapting as you go. Third, imaginative analysis: bringing creativity to how you read and interpret. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: When you face a blank page at the start of an essay or project, the hardest part is often not the writing but finding and shaping ideas. Creative methods give you a way in. This lesson looks at visual and mapping methods, such as mind maps, that help you generate ideas quickly and then organise them into a structure you can work from.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You already accept that creativity has a place in academic work. The aim now is to put a method into practice on your own task, not just to agree that generating ideas matters. You will try a mapping method and see how it turns a scatter of thoughts into a working plan.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: use a visual mapping method to generate ideas for a piece of academic work
organise generated ideas into a structure you can work from
select a creative method that fits an academic task in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A visual mapping method puts a central idea in the middle of the page and grows branches of related ideas outward from it. Mind mapping is the best known: you write the topic at the centre, branch out with subtopics, and branch again from each of those. Because you are not writing in straight lines, you can add ideas in any order and see how they connect.

The method does two jobs. First, it helps you generate: branching invites more ideas than a list does, and you hold back judgement while the map grows. Second, it helps you organise: once the ideas are down, the branches show you groupings and an order you can turn into a plan.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a piece of work you are about to start. How do you usually gather your first ideas, and what might a mind map add? What is one task you could try mapping next?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Creative methods give you a way into academic work when ideas are hard to find. A visual mapping method, such as a mind map, helps you generate ideas by branching from a central topic, and then organise them by grouping the branches into a structure. You can now use a mapping method, shape its output into a plan, and choose a method that fits the task. The next lesson widens this from one method to generating several approaches.

title: Orientation
body: A creative worker rarely takes the first approach that comes to mind and sticks with it whatever happens. They generate several ways in, try one, watch how it goes, and change course if it is not working. This lesson is about that flexibility: producing more than one approach to a task, and adapting as you go.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You can already generate ideas. The step here is to treat your approach itself as something to choose and change, not fix at the start. You will practise producing several approaches to one task and deciding, as you work, whether to keep going or switch.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: generate several different approaches to the same academic task
monitor whether an approach is working as you apply it
adapt or switch your approach when a task in {{context}} is not going to plan.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Flexible thinking has two parts. The first is generating options: before you commit, you deliberately produce more than one way to tackle a task, rather than running with the first. A problem usually has several routes through it, and the first route is not always the best.

The second part is monitoring and adapting. As you work, you keep checking whether your approach is actually getting you anywhere. If one strategy is not working, you amend it or choose another you think will work better. Creativity here is not a single flash of inspiration. It is the habit of keeping your options open and staying ready to change.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent task where your first approach ran into trouble. Did you push on or change course? What other approach could you have tried, and how would you have known to switch?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Thinking flexibly has two parts: generating several approaches to a task before you commit, and monitoring your chosen approach so you can adapt or switch when it is not working. You can now produce more than one way into a task, watch how an approach is going, and change course with control rather than pushing on regardless. The next lesson turns creativity onto the material itself, bringing imagination to analysis.

title: Orientation
body: Creativity is not only for generating ideas and approaches. It also shapes how you read and interpret. An imaginative reader does not just report what a source says. They open it up, ask what it might mean, and connect it to ideas the source itself never mentioned. This lesson brings creative thinking to analysis and interpretation.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You have used creative methods to generate ideas and approaches. Now you apply the same imagination to the material in front of you. The aim is to produce original connections and readings, not simply to summarise, while keeping your interpretation grounded in the source.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: apply imaginative thinking to open up an interpretation rather than take it at face value
produce an original connection between ideas or sources
distinguish an imaginative, creative reading of a source in {{context}} from a routine one.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Analysis means breaking an interpretation, a body of evidence or a data set down through close examination. Imaginative analysis adds something to that. Instead of only taking the parts apart, you ask what else they could mean, what they connect to, and what question the source leaves open.

Opening up the discourse is the key move. A routine reader treats a source as a closed statement to record. An imaginative reader treats it as a starting point, bringing in other ideas and making connections the source did not state. The imagination is not a licence to invent. A creative reading is still anchored in the text and the evidence, but it reaches further than a summary does.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a source you read recently. Did you only summarise it, or did you ask what else it could mean and what it connected to? What is one connection you could have made?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Imaginative analysis brings creativity to how you read. You examine a source closely, then open it up: asking what it could mean, making original connections, and bringing in ideas the source never stated, while staying anchored in the evidence. You can now tell an imaginative reading from a routine one and produce connections of your own. Across the course you have put creative methods to work: generating and organising ideas, thinking flexibly across approaches, and reading with imagination.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Creativity is no longer a vague quality but a set of methods you can use. You can generate and organise ideas with visual mapping, produce several approaches to a task and adapt when one is not working, and bring imaginative thinking to how you analyse and interpret sources. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, creative methods are something you practise in every module. Each essay you map out, each task you approach more than one way, each source you read for what it could mean, puts these methods to work. The same methods drive creative problem-solving in professional life, where generating options, adapting and seeing fresh connections are valued everywhere.

body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced creativity course takes these methods towards innovation, enterprise and the creative attributes that graduate and professional work reward. If you want the foundations, the introductory creativity course covers what creativity is at university. Going wider: the same methods support Academic Writing, Researching and Revising, where you put creativity to work on real tasks.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four practices that make a mind map generate and then organise your ideas.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Start from the centre
_items.subtitle: Generate
_items.text: Put your topic in the middle of the page and branch outward. Working from a centre invites more ideas than a top-to-bottom list, because any branch can grow at any time.

_items.title: Hold back judgement
_items.subtitle: Generate
_items.text: While the map is growing, add ideas without deciding yet whether they are good. Aim for quantity first; you can weigh and cut later. Judging too early stops ideas coming.

_items.title: Group the branches
_items.subtitle: Organise
_items.text: Once the ideas are down, look for branches that belong together. Grouping related ideas turns a scatter of thoughts into a handful of themes you can build on.

_items.title: Turn the map into a plan
_items.subtitle: Organise
_items.text: Read the groups in a sensible order and you have the outline of your work. The map that generated your ideas becomes the structure that organises them.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students planning the same essay from a blank page.

{{learner-a}} writes a quick list of points down the page, settles on the first three that seem usable, and starts drafting. The plan is done fast. But the list closed down early: {{learner-a}} took the first ideas that came and never saw how they might connect or what was missing. The essay stays thin.

{{learner-b}} puts the essay question in the centre of a page and branches outward, adding ideas freely without judging them yet. With the map full, {{learner-b}} looks for branches that group together, names a few themes, and orders them into a plan. The same blank page has produced a richer, better-organised essay.

Both students planned the same essay. Only {{learner-b}} used a method that generated ideas widely and then organised them, rather than settling on the first few.

title: Practical guidance
body: These moves turn a blank page into a mapped plan. Try them on your next piece of work.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I written my topic in the centre and started branching outward?
Have I kept adding ideas before stopping to judge them?
Have I aimed for quantity first, rather than settling on my first idea?
Have I looked for branches that group together into themes?
Have I put the groups into an order I can write from?
Have I chosen a method that suits this task, rather than always using the same one?

_items.text: It makes your plan look neater on the page.

_items.feedback: A map keeps order open while you generate, the opposite of fixed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what branching does that a straight list cannot.

_items.feedback: Speed of drafting is not how ideas get organised.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student grouped the branches into themes and ordered them into a plan.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four stages that turn a single fixed approach into flexible working. Reveal each stage in turn.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal how flexible working unfolds.

_items.title: Generate approaches
_items.body: Before you start, list two or three different ways you could tackle the task. Resist running with the first idea; give yourself a choice.

_items.title: Choose and try one
_items.body: Pick the approach that looks most promising and begin. Trying an approach is the only way to find out whether it really works.

_items.title: Monitor as you go
_items.body: Keep asking whether this is getting you anywhere. Notice early if you are stuck or the work is drifting from the task.

_items.title: Adapt or switch
_items.body: If the approach is not working, amend it or go back to one of your other options. Changing course is a sign of control, not failure.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students are set the same demanding assignment with a tight deadline.

{{learner-a}} picks the first approach that comes to mind and commits to it. Half way through, it is clearly not working, but {{learner-a}} pushes on the same way, hoping effort alone will fix it. Time runs out with little to show. There was never a second option to turn to.

{{learner-b}} starts by jotting three ways the assignment could be tackled, then tries the most promising one. Watching the work stall, {{learner-b}} stops, returns to the list, and switches to another approach that fits better. The task gets finished, because a change of course was always available.

Both students worked hard. Only {{learner-b}} generated options and stayed ready to adapt, turning a stall into a switch rather than a dead end.

title: Practical guidance
body: These moves keep your approach flexible. Try them on your next task.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I listed more than one approach before starting?
Have I chosen the approach that looks most promising, rather than just the first?
Have I checked, as I work, whether the approach is getting me anywhere?
Have I noticed early when an approach has stalled?
Have I been willing to amend or switch rather than push on regardless?
Have I kept my other options in mind in case I need them?

title: Formative check: generating approaches
displayTitle: What does thinking flexibly ask you to do at the start of a task?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does flexible thinking ask you to do at the start of a task?

_items.text: Generate several possible approaches, rather than running with the first that comes to mind.
_items.feedback: Yes. Produce a choice of approaches before you commit.

_items.text: Commit to the first approach and see it through.
_items.feedback: Committing to the first idea is the opposite of flexible thinking.

_items.text: Ask someone else to choose your approach for you.
_items.feedback: Flexibility is about generating your own options, not handing the choice over.

_items.text: Delay starting until the deadline is close.
_items.feedback: Delay is not flexibility; generating options is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Flexible thinking means generating several approaches before you commit.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What should you do before settling on one way in?
_incorrect.final: Flexible thinking asks you to generate several approaches first. Committing to the first, handing the choice over or delaying are not flexible moves.

title: Formative check: monitoring an approach
displayTitle: In the worked example, what let the second student realise their first approach was not working?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What let the second student realise their approach was not working?

_items.text: They kept checking, as they worked, whether the approach was getting them anywhere.
_items.feedback: Yes. Monitoring the work is what revealed the stall.

_items.text: They waited until the deadline to review it.
_items.feedback: Waiting until the end is too late to adapt; monitoring happens as you work.

_items.text: They asked the first student what to do.
_items.feedback: The realisation came from their own monitoring, not from asking.

_items.text: They had chosen only one approach from the start.
_items.feedback: Having one approach is the first student's problem, not how the second noticed the stall.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Monitoring the work as they went is what let the second student spot the stall.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What were they doing while they worked that the first student was not?
_incorrect.final: The second student kept checking, as they worked, whether the approach was getting anywhere. That monitoring revealed the stall in time to switch.

title: Formative check: adapting
displayTitle: You are part-way through a task in {{context}} and your approach has clearly stalled. What is the flexible move?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the flexible move when an approach has stalled?

_items.text: Amend the approach, or switch to another one you think will work better.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, changing course under control is the flexible move.

_items.text: Keep going the same way and hope it comes good.
_items.feedback: Pushing on regardless is what the first student did, and it failed.

_items.text: Stop working on the task altogether.
_items.feedback: Flexibility means switching approach, not abandoning the task.

_items.text: Start again from a blank page with no plan.
_items.feedback: You can return to your other options rather than start from nothing.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, amending or switching your approach is the flexible response to a stall.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What keeps you moving when one approach is not working?
_incorrect.final: The flexible move in {{context}} is to amend the approach or switch to another. Pushing on, stopping or starting blank are not flexible responses.

title: Explore the concept
instruction: Select the card to reveal the definition, an example and related terms.
definition: Reading a source for what it could mean and connect to, not only for what it plainly says.
extendedDefinition: It breaks an interpretation down through close examination, then opens it up by bringing in other ideas and making original connections, while staying anchored in the evidence.
example: An imaginative reader of a study asks what it implies for a case the authors never discussed, and links it to a theory from another module.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students write about the same interpretation of a well-known source.

{{learner-a}} reports the interpretation accurately: this is what the author argues, and this is the evidence given. The summary is correct and clear. But it stops there. {{learner-a}} records what the source says and adds nothing, so the reader learns the source but not what to make of it.

{{learner-b}} examines the same interpretation closely, then opens it up. What else could this mean? {{learner-b}} connects it to an idea from another source the author never mentions, and offers an original reading, still anchored in the evidence. The source becomes a starting point, not a closed statement.

Both students understood the source. Only {{learner-b}} read it imaginatively, making a connection of their own rather than only summarising.

_items.text: Have I examined the source closely before interpreting it?
Have I asked what the source could mean, beyond what it plainly states?
Have I brought in another idea or source to open up the discussion?
Have I made a connection the source itself did not make?
Have I kept my reading anchored in the evidence, rather than inventing?
Have I checked whether I am interpreting the source or only summarising it?

title: Formative check: imaginative versus routine
displayTitle: What makes a reading of a source imaginative rather than routine?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What makes a reading of a source imaginative rather than routine?

_items.text: It opens the source up, asking what it could mean and what it connects to.
_items.feedback: Yes. Opening up and connecting is the imaginative move.

_items.text: It reports what the source says as accurately as possible.
_items.feedback: Accurate reporting is a routine reading, not an imaginative one.

_items.text: It uses longer quotations from the source.
_items.feedback: More quotation is still reporting, not interpreting.

_items.text: It avoids the source's evidence entirely.
_items.feedback: An imaginative reading stays anchored in the evidence, not away from it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An imaginative reading opens the source up and connects it, rather than only recording it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What does an imaginative reader do beyond reporting the source?
_incorrect.final: An imaginative reading opens the source up, asking what it could mean and connect to. Accurate reporting, longer quotes or ignoring the evidence are not imaginative analysis.

title: Formative check: an original connection
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's reading more than a summary?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's reading more than a summary?

_items.text: They connected the source to another idea and produced an original reading grounded in the text.
_items.feedback: Yes. The original connection, anchored in the text, is what went beyond summary.

_items.text: They reported the author's argument more accurately.
_items.feedback: Accurate reporting is still a summary.

_items.text: They wrote at greater length about the source.
_items.feedback: Length does not turn a summary into imaginative analysis.

_items.text: They quoted the author's own conclusion.
_items.feedback: Quoting the author still reports the source rather than interpreting it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student made an original connection, grounded in the text, which goes beyond summarising.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student added that the first did not.
_incorrect.final: The second student's reading went beyond summary because they made an original connection to another idea, anchored in the text. Accuracy, length or quotation do not.

title: Formative check: spotting imaginative analysis
displayTitle: You are reading a key source in {{context}}. Which response shows imaginative analysis rather than a routine reading?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response shows imaginative analysis rather than a routine reading?

_items.text: Asking what the source could mean and linking it to another idea, while staying anchored in the evidence.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, opening up and connecting, anchored in evidence, is imaginative analysis.

_items.text: Summarising the source as accurately as you can.
_items.feedback: Accurate summary is a routine reading.

_items.text: Copying the source's main claim into your notes.
_items.feedback: Copying records the source; it does not interpret it.

_items.text: Inventing a claim the source does not support.
_items.feedback: Imagination is not invention; a creative reading stays anchored.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, opening the source up and connecting it, anchored in evidence, is imaginative analysis.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which response reaches beyond the source while staying grounded in it?
_incorrect.final: In {{context}}, imaginative analysis asks what the source could mean and links it to another idea, anchored in the evidence. Summarising, copying or inventing are not imaginative analysis.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: generating and organising ideas with visual maps, thinking flexibly across several approaches, and bringing imagination to how you analyse sources. On their own they are three separate methods. This lesson brings them together into one way of working.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to work creatively on every task at once. The aim is to see these methods as one creative practice rather than three separate techniques, so creativity carries on into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect idea-mapping, flexible thinking and imaginative analysis as one creative way of working
analyse how the three creative methods work as one across a student's academic project
apply the three together to keep working creatively on your {{context}} study beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Working creatively is creativity made a way of working, not a one-off trick for a single task. It is one practice with three moves: generate and organise your ideas, produce several approaches and adapt as you go, and read your material with imagination. The three methods from the earlier lessons are the parts of that one practice.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, you do not pick one creative method and stop. On a single piece of work you might map your ideas, weigh up two or three ways to approach it, and read your sources for what they could mean. The methods support one another when you use them together.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of work you have coming up. How could you bring all three methods to it: mapping your ideas, trying several approaches, and reading your sources imaginatively? When will you start?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Creativity is most useful when it becomes one way of working, not a set of separate tricks. On any task you can map and organise your ideas, try several approaches and adapt, and read with imagination, all together. It is using the methods together, across your studies, that strengthens your work.

title: The practice as one cycle
body: Working creatively is a continuing way of working, not a one-off trick. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Map ideas
_items.body: Map out and organise your ideas, branching from a central topic.

_items.title: Generate
_items.body: Generate several different approaches to the task rather than taking the first.

_items.title: Adapt
_items.body: As you work, check how your approach is going and adapt or switch it when it stalls.

_items.title: Read imaginatively
_items.body: Read your sources imaginatively, opening them up and making original connections that feed fresh ideas back into the cycle.

_diagram.title: Working creatively as a continuing practice

title: Worked example
body: Two students tackle the same assignment. One reaches for a single method, lists a few points, and writes the whole thing one way through. The other maps ideas first, tries two approaches and drops the weaker, then reads each source for fresh connections. The second piece of work is richer, because the methods were used together rather than one at a time.

title: Working with the cycle
body: Use these to keep creativity running across a whole task, rather than reaching for one trick and stopping.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I map and organise my ideas before settling on a plan?
Did I produce more than one approach rather than run with the first?
Did I watch how my approach was going and adapt when it stalled?
Did I read my material imaginatively, not just summarise it?
Did I use these methods together, rather than treating them as separate tricks?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat these creative methods as one way of working rather than three separate techniques?
body: Why is it more useful to treat these creative methods as one way of working rather than three separate techniques?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat these creative methods as one way of working rather than three separate techniques?

_items.text: Because they support each other: mapping feeds your approaches, staying flexible keeps them open, and imaginative reading deepens the whole task.
_items.feedback: Yes. Used together, the three methods strengthen one piece of work.

_items.text: Because using one method at a time is always faster than using several.
_items.feedback: Speed is not the point. The methods are stronger used together.

_items.text: Because only one of the three methods actually helps academic work.
_items.feedback: All three help. The gain comes from using them together.

_items.text: Because treating them separately means you never have to adapt your approach.
_items.feedback: Adapting your approach is one of the methods, not something to avoid.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three methods work as one creative way of working, each supporting the others.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you gain by using the three methods together on one task.

displayTitle: A student plans an essay with a mind map, tries two different arguments, drops the weaker one, and reads each source for what it could mean. What does this show?
body: A student plans an essay with a mind map, tries two different arguments, drops the weaker one, and reads each source for what it could mean. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student plans an essay with a mind map, tries two different arguments, drops the weaker one, and reads each source for what it could mean. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three creative methods are working together as one way of working on a single task.
_items.feedback: Yes. Mapping, flexible thinking and imaginative reading are all in play at once.

_items.text: That the student used only one creative method and ignored the rest.
_items.feedback: Look again: mapping, flexible thinking and imaginative reading all appear.

_items.text: That mind mapping cannot be combined with other methods.
_items.feedback: The example shows mapping combined with the other two methods.

_items.text: That creativity belongs only at the planning stage of an essay.
_items.feedback: Creativity runs on here from planning through to reading the sources.

_feedback.correct: That's right. All three methods are at work together across one piece of work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how many of the three methods the student used.

displayTitle: You want to work more creatively in your {{context}} study this term. Which plan best uses the three methods together as one way of working?
body: You want to work more creatively in your {{context}} study this term. Which plan best uses the three methods together as one way of working?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to work more creatively in your your subject study this term. Which plan best uses the three methods together as one way of working?

_items.text: On each task, map and organise your ideas, try several approaches and adapt, and read your sources imaginatively.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three methods together, task after task.

_items.text: Pick whichever single method you like best and use only that one all term.
_items.feedback: Using one method alone misses the gain of working them together.

_items.text: Use a mind map once at the start of term and nothing else after that.
_items.feedback: One map at the start is not a continuing creative way of working.

_items.text: Wait until an assignment goes wrong before trying anything creative.
_items.feedback: Creative working is something you plan from the start, not a last resort.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Using the three methods together, on task after task, is working creatively across your study.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which plan uses all three methods together, again and again?

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What does it mean to treat creativity as one way of working rather than three separate methods?
body: What does it mean to treat creativity as one way of working rather than three separate methods?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to treat creativity as one way of working rather than three separate methods?

_items.text: You bring mapping, flexible thinking and imaginative analysis to the same task, using them together.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three methods work together on one piece of work.

_items.text: You choose one of the three methods and use only it.
_items.feedback: That keeps the methods separate rather than working them together.

_items.text: You use creativity only when planning, never when reading.
_items.feedback: A creative way of working runs through reading too.

_items.text: You stop adapting your approach once a task is under way.
_items.feedback: Adapting is part of the practice, not something to drop.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
